questions.question: Web accessibility only benefits people who are permanently blind.
questions.explanation: Accessibility also helps people with temporary disabilities (broken arm), situational limitations (bright sunlight), and a wide range of other permanent disabilities.

questions.question: Placeholder text can be used as a replacement for a visible `<label>`.
questions.explanation: Placeholder text disappears when the user starts typing and often fails WCAG contrast requirements. A persistent label is required.

questions.question: Adding `role="button"` to a `<div>` automatically makes it respond to the Enter and Space keys.
questions.explanation: ARIA adds no behaviour. You must write JavaScript keyboard handlers to mimic a button's functionality.

questions.question: Captions are required for prerecorded video at WCAG Level A.
questions.explanation: Success Criterion 1.2.2 (Captions) is a Level A requirement.

questions.question: A `role="alert"` live region will wait politely until the screen reader is idle before speaking.
questions.explanation: `role="alert"` implies `aria-live="assertive"`, which interrupts the current speech immediately.

questions.question: In a roving tabindex pattern, every item in the group should have `tabindex="0"`.
questions.explanation: Only one item at a time has `tabindex="0"`; the rest are set to `tabindex="-1"` so that the group acts as a single tab stop.

questions.question: Automated testing tools can detect approximately 80% of all accessibility issues.
questions.explanation: Automated tools typically catch only around 20‑30% of issues; manual and user testing are essential.

questions.question: The `<details>` and `<summary>` elements provide an accessible disclosure widget without any JavaScript.
questions.explanation: These native HTML elements are keyboard‑accessible, announced by screen readers, and require no custom scripting.
